CausalChain: Chronic viral infection/oxidative stress -> Upregulation of m6A methyltransferases -> Enhanced deposition of m6A (and co-occurring modifications) on specific lncRNAs -> Altered lncRNA secondary structure -> Enhanced binding to epigenetic regulators (e.g., EZH2) -> Recruitment of chromatin remodeling complexes -> Epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes -> Promotion of HCC proliferation and metastasis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, chronic viral infection and oxidative stress trigger an overexpression of m6A methyltransferases, leading to increased m6A modification on a select group of lncRNAs. These modifications alter the lncRNA secondary structure, thereby switching their binding affinity towards epigenetic modifiers such as EZH2. This altered interaction recruits chromatin remodeling complexes that epigenetically silence tumor suppressor genes. Furthermore, we propose that additional RNA modifications (e.g., m7G and m5C) may act in concert with m6A to fine-tune this molecular switch. The use of CRISPR/Cas-based epitranscriptomic editing, combined with high-throughput RIP-seq and RNA structural assays, will allow us to precisely map and manipulate this pathway, confirming the direct causal relationship between m6A-modified lncRNA interaction dynamics and HCC progression.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), chronic viral infection and oxidative stress initiate an upregulation of m6A methyltransferases, resulting in heightened deposition of m6A marks on a defined subset of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). We hypothesize that these m6A modifications, potentially in concert with additional RNA modifications (e.g., m7G and m5C), induce conformational changes in lncRNAs that enhance their affinity for epigenetic regulators, such as EZH2. This enhanced binding facilitates the recruitment of chromatin remodeling complexes, leading to the epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes and promoting oncogenic processes. Leveraging contemporary technologies—including CRISPR/Cas-mediated epitranscriptomic editing, high-throughput RIP-seq, and advanced RNA structure probing—we propose to delineate the causal steps underlying the functional switch of lncRNAs from tumor-suppressive to oncogenic, thereby providing a precise mechanistic understanding and identifying novel therapeutic targets in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that m6A modifications act as a regulatory switch converting tumor-suppressive lncRNAs into oncogenic mediators via altered binding to epigenetic regulators. The revised hypothesis retains this core idea but enhances specificity by integrating additional RNA modifications (m7G and m5C) as potential cooperative factors and specifying the involvement of particular epigenetic regulators (e.g., EZH2). Furthermore, contemporary technological strategies such as CRISPR/Cas-mediated epitranscriptomic editing and high-throughput sequencing-based assays have been incorporated to bolster the practical implementability and mechanistic dissection of the causal chain. Each step of the original causal chain—from stress-induced methyltransferase upregulation to altered lncRNA interactions and epigenetic silencing—is explicitly maintained and expanded upon to offer a more comprehensive and testable model.
